This page holds the exercise of the course, Tasks 1 to 6, on a copy of R that runs inside your browser, with the data already in place. It is the fallback when a live deck does not load or an installation fails, and it gives the same numbers as the decks and the downloadable workspace.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## While the R engine loads

The R engine downloads into your browser when you open this page (a minute or so, longer on a slow connection). It is ready when the first code cell shows a "Run Code" button. Keep this tab open, because your work is lost when the page is refreshed.
:::

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
#| output: false
# Runs by itself once the engine is ready: the Housing data as `housing`, one
# row per email, and the folder from which the helpers read their files.
.data_dir <- "data"
housing <- utils::read.csv("data/housing_emails.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
```

{{< include _includes/_lab-helpers.qmd >}}

Five analysts reanalysed a claim of the Housing case study [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] for the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]; you are analyst no. 6. The claim is that "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts", in the words of the original authors (OAs) as selected by the SCORE programme. The [background page](background.qmd) presents the original study, the robustness study and the five reanalyses.

The pages of your format say which of the six tasks it covers, and whether it sends anything to the class chart.

## Task 1 – The setup check {#task-1-setup}

Press **Run Code** on the cell below.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
writeLines(c(
  paste("R is running in your browser:", R.version.string),
  sprintf("The emails are loaded: %d rows", nrow(housing)),
  sprintf("The estimator reproduces the reference specification: %.2f percentage points",
          fit_spec(housing)$b_pp)))
```

You should see **1,014 rows** and, on the last line, **−19.97 percentage points**. If not, reload the page, wait for the engine and run the cell again. If it still fails, open the page in another browser.

## Warm-up – the three Rs {#warm-up}

Three of the four scenarios below describe one of the three Rs (reproducibility, robustness, replicability), and the fourth describes something else. Read all four, then fill in the gaps in the code cell and run it.

***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer runs the Stata `.do` file of the OAs on their public data file and gets a coefficient for Hispanic names that differs from the one printed in the paper, because the public file holds the size, poverty and ethnic composition of each community in thirds rather than as the census values. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though the numbers do not match.

***Scenario 2:*** An analyst takes the same public file, re-implements the analysis in R instead of Stata, and also counts the five replies that carry no greeting code as replies without a greeting. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?

***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team emails 3,050 public housing authorities with four new names and finds no difference in how often the replies greet the sender by name. Their conclusion is that the original finding has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_.

***Scenario 4:*** Another researcher asks whether the same bias appears when people telephone school districts rather than email housing authorities, codes recorded voice messages instead of written replies, and finds the same pattern. The researcher concludes that the original finding \_\_\_\_\_\_ to another service and another medium.

```{webr}
#| exercise: vocab
#| code-overflow: wrap
writeLines(c(
  "Scenario 1: This is an example of ______.",
  "Scenario 2: Is this a case of ______ or ______?",
  "Scenario 3: The original finding has failed to ______.",
  "Scenario 4: The original finding ______ to another service and another medium."
))
```

:::: {.solution exercise="vocab"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Answers

1.  **reproducibility** – rerunning the code of the OAs on their data. The numbers differ, but the activity is still reproduction, and the difference has a documented cause: the blinded file.
2.  a grey area. Re-implementing on the same data in different software is still **reproducibility**, but recoding the uncoded replies is an analytic choice, which makes it a test of **robustness**.
3.  **replicability** – the same question asked of independent new data.
4.  **generalises** (generalisability) – the odd one out, with a new population, new data and a new measure at once.
:::
::::

## Task 2 – The data {#task-2-data}

The **Housing data** are loaded as `housing`, one row per email, and the [codebook](data/housing_emails_codebook.md) describes every column. Run the cell below to count what came back.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# How many emails, and what came back?
housing |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails    = n(),
                           bounced   = sum(is.na(reply)),
                           delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)),
                           replies   = sum(reply %in% 1),
                           coded     = sum(!is.na(named)))
```

You should find **1,014 emails** (the paper reports 1,017, three more than the public file holds), of which **23 bounced** and never reached an official, **991 delivered**, **563 replies**, and **558 replies with a greeting code**. The column `reply` is 1 for a reply, 0 for none and missing for a bounced email. `named` is 1 when a reply greeted the sender by name, 0 when it did not, and missing for every email without a reply and for the five replies that carry no greeting code.

Now the replies and the greetings by the group of the name:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(delivered   = n(),
                           replies     = sum(reply == 1),
                           coded       = sum(!is.na(named)),
                           greeted     = sum(named %in% 1),
                           greeted_pct = round(100 * sum(named %in% 1) / sum(!is.na(named)), 1),
                           by = "group")
```

Tables print on this page as plain text. For a formatted table, add `|> gt::gt()` to the end of the cell and run it again.

Then the share greeted by name for each of the six names. This cell works out the shares and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# The share greeted by name for each of the six names, from the lowest
greeted <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(greeted_pct = 100 * mean(named), by = c("group", "name")) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("greeted_pct") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(group = factor(group, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic"),
                                         labels = c("white", "Black", "Hispanic")))
```

The next cell draws them, a bar for each name with its share at the end.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
tinyplot::tinyplot(greeted_pct ~ name | group, data = greeted,
                   type = tinyplot::type_barplot(xlevels = greeted$name, width = 0.7, drop.zeros = TRUE), flip = TRUE,
                   palette = c("grey60", "#4a78ab", "#8b1538"), fill = "by",
                   legend = list("right!", title = "Names meant to indicate"),
                   xlab = NA, ylab = "Replies that greeted the sender by name (%)",
                   ylim = c(0, 72), theme = "minimal")
# the share at the end of each bar
tinyplot::tinyplot(x = seq_len(nrow(greeted)), y = greeted$greeted_pct, flip = TRUE,
                   type = tinyplot::type_text(labels = sprintf("%.1f%%", greeted$greeted_pct), pos = 4),
                   cex = 0.9, add = TRUE)
```

The replies to white names greeted the sender by name in 61.1% of cases, those to Hispanic names in 41.2%: a gap of about 20 points, the size of the published estimate. Black names fall in between, at 56.1%, and of the six names Santiago received the fewest greetings by name.

## Task 2, continued – The estimand and the graph {#task-2-estimand-and-graph}

Before fitting anything, say what you are trying to estimate, in words. A template that you can adapt:

> The **unit-specific quantity** is, for each housing authority, the difference between whether it would come back with a reply that greets the sender by name to an email signed with a Hispanic name and to the same email signed with a white name. The **target population** is the public housing authorities that received an email.

There is a catch in that sentence. An authority whose official would not reply to one of the names has no greeting to compare. The comparison can then count every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting, or count the replies only, which compares the authorities that replied to Hispanic names with those that replied to white names. These need not be the same authorities.

A causal graph makes the catch visible. Its nodes are variables, its arrows run from cause to effect, and the rules for reading it say which paths between the name and the greeting are open, given what the comparison conditions on.

{{< include _includes/_lab-graph.qmd >}}

The cell below builds the graph, one arrow to a string, with the reason for each arrow in a comment, and prints nothing. One arrow is switched off with a `#`: the arrow from the name to the greeting, which is the effect on tone that the claim is about.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_dag <- make_dag(
  # The name can affect whether the official replies at all.
  "name -> reply",
  # Only a reply can greet the sender by name.
  "reply -> greeting",
  # The official, whom nobody observed, affects both the reply and the greeting.
  "official -> reply",
  "official -> greeting",
  # So does the community of the housing authority, held in thirds in the data.
  "community -> reply",
  "community -> greeting",

  # The effect on tone that the claim is about: take the # off if you believe it.
  # "name -> greeting",

  exposure = "name", outcome = "greeting", latent = "official"
)
```

Two questions are put to the graph. On this page `adjustmentSets()` and `paths()` print the answers that dagitty, the R package for causal graphs, gives for this graph, with and without the arrow of the claim ([codebook](data/dag_answers_codebook.md)); any other graph gets a pointer to the workspace, where dagitty itself runs. The first question is what has to be adjusted for when the comparison counts every delivered email:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
adjustmentSets(my_dag)
```

The second is which paths from the name to the greeting are open once the comparison is made among replies only, which is what `Z = "reply"` asks: it conditions on the reply.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
paths(my_dag, Z = "reply")
```

The last cell draws the graph.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_dag(my_dag)
```

`adjustmentSets()` returns `{}`, the empty set: nothing has to be adjusted for, because nothing points into the name. The names were assigned at random, so no common cause of the name and the greeting can exist. Conditioning on the reply changes the picture. The path through the reply closes, but two paths open, one through the community and one through the official, because the reply is a common effect of the name and of each of them (a collider), and comparing replies only conditions on it. This is the problem of conditioning on a consequence of the treatment, which @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias sets out for audit experiments.

Now take the `#` off the arrow `"name -> greeting"` in the cell that builds the graph, and run that cell and the three after it again. Then run the cell below, which also adjusts for the community. Answer three questions for your own notes: why the adjustment set stays empty; which paths stay open among replies once the community is adjusted for, and what that means for a gap among replies; and which emails keep the comparison randomised.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
paths(my_dag, Z = c("reply", "community"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers

1.  The set stays `{}` because nothing points into the name, whatever arrows leave it: the names were randomised.
2.  The direct path and the path through the official stay open. A gap among replies mixes the effect of the name on tone with differences between the officials who reply to each name, and adjusting for the community cannot remove the second, because the official is unobserved.
3.  Every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting. That comparison estimates the effect of the name on receiving a greeting by name at all, which mixes the decision to reply with the tone of the reply.

The difference between the two comparisons is the decision on which emails are counted, the second argument of `try_spec()` in Task 4, and whatever you conclude here belongs in field 4 of your preregistration in Task 5.
:::

## Task 3 – The reproduction {#task-3-reproduction}

This is the **reproducibility** check. Five analysts reanalysed the claim for the robustness study, each with code of their own, and the robustness study recorded a test statistic for four of them. Reproduce the analysis of one of the five from the public file of the OAs, `housing_original.csv`, which keeps their column names. `Response_Dichotomous` is 1 for a reply, 0 for none and empty for a bounced email. `ProperName` is the greeting by name, empty for every email that has no reply with a greeting code. `TreatmentGroup` holds the group and the sex of the name (`"Hispanic male"`, `"white female"` and so on).

| Analyst | What the analysis compared | Emails counted | Test | Recorded in the robustness study |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [8PTRZ](#task-3-8ptrz) | Hispanic names against all other names | the 558 replies with a greeting code | chi-square test of a 2 × 2 table | $\chi^2$ = 14.265 |
| [UYV3F](#task-3-uyv3f) | Hispanic against white names | the 362 coded replies to those names | logistic regression without covariates | z = −3.771 |
| [EWFMI](#task-3-ewfmi) | the three groups, with Hispanic names as the base | the 549 coded replies that carry a poverty third | logistic regression with the sex of the name, the poverty third and the hard-to-find address | z = 3.645 |
| [25N5D](#task-3-25n5d) | Hispanic against white names | the 665 delivered emails to those names, a missing reply counted as no greeting | two-proportion test | $\chi^2$ = 13.683 |
| [P9W8Y](#task-3-p9w8y) | the three groups | the 558 replies with a greeting code | likelihood-ratio test of a logistic regression | none |

Each analyst has a few cells below, one step each, to be run in order. One cell of each analyst is an exercise: replace the blank (`______`) with the missing code, then press "Run Code". A hint and the solution sit under that cell.

Whichever analyst you reproduce, run the cell below first. It reads the public file as `original` and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
original <- utils::read.csv("data/housing_original.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
```

### 8PTRZ – the test of a table {#task-3-8ptrz}

```{webr}
#| exercise: repro-8ptrz
#| envir: global
# keep the replies that carry a greeting code, and mark the Hispanic names
coded_replies <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(______)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
```

:::: {.hint exercise="repro-8ptrz"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the replies with a greeting code

`ProperName` is empty for every email without a reply, for the bounced emails and for the five replies without a greeting code, so keeping the rows in which it is not missing leaves the 558 coded replies.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="repro-8ptrz"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
coded_replies <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
```
:::
::::

Then run the next two cells in order.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the 2 x 2 table: Hispanic or other name, by greeting
tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded_replies)
tab_8ptrz
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the chi-square test of the table
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)
```

You should get `X-squared = 14.265, df = 1`, the value on record for 8PTRZ.

### UYV3F – a logistic regression {#task-3-uyv3f}

The first cell keeps the rows of the analysis and prints nothing. The second, the exercise, fits the model.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the coded replies to Hispanic and white names, with the Hispanic names marked
replies_uyv3f <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName) & !grepl("^black", TreatmentGroup)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: repro-uyv3f
#| envir: global
# the logistic regression of the greeting on the name
m_uyv3f <- glm(ProperName ~ hispanic_name, family = ______(), data = replies_uyv3f)
nobs(m_uyv3f)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="repro-uyv3f"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the family of the model

A logistic regression is a generalised linear model of a 0/1 outcome with the family that R calls `binomial`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="repro-uyv3f"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
m_uyv3f <- glm(ProperName ~ hispanic_name, family = binomial(), data = replies_uyv3f)
nobs(m_uyv3f)
```
:::
::::

The last cell prints the coefficients.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the coefficients, with the z of each
print(parameters::model_parameters(m_uyv3f, ci_method = "wald"), digits = 3)
```

The row of the Hispanic names gives z = −3.771 on 362 replies, the value on record for UYV3F.

The analyst compared the other groups with the Hispanic names, so `"Hispanic"` comes first among the levels, spelled as in `TreatmentGroup`.

``` r
replies_ewfmi <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_separate(select = "TreatmentGroup", new_columns = c("ethnicity", "name_sex"),

```

### P9W8Y – a test of three groups {#task-3-p9w8y}

The robustness study recorded no statistic for this analysis, so the rerun cannot be matched against the record. The report that the analyst filed gives $\chi^2$ = 15.951 on 2 degrees of freedom in its text.

The first cell keeps the coded replies and prints nothing, the second fits the model, and the third, the exercise, tests it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the coded replies, with the group of the name as a factor
replies_p9w8y <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_separate(select = "TreatmentGroup", new_columns = c("ethnicity", "name_sex"),
                            separator = " ", append = TRUE) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(ethnicity = factor(ethnicity, levels = c("white", "black", "Hispanic")))
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the model of the three groups
m_p9w8y <- glm(ProperName ~ ethnicity, family = binomial(), data = replies_p9w8y)
nobs(m_p9w8y)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: repro-p9w8y
#| envir: global
# the likelihood-ratio test against the same model without the groups
anova(update(m_p9w8y, . ~ 1), m_p9w8y, test = "______")
```

:::: {.hint exercise="repro-p9w8y"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the test

`anova()` compares two nested models fitted to the same rows; a likelihood-ratio test is asked for with `test = "LRT"`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="repro-p9w8y"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
anova(update(m_p9w8y, . ~ 1), m_p9w8y, test = "LRT")
```

The column `Deviance` gives 15.951 on 2 degrees of freedom for 558 replies, the value of the report.
:::
::::

### Defaults and codings {#task-3-defaults}

Now find out why your number is exactly that number. For a 2 × 2 table, `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` both apply the continuity correction of Yates unless they are told otherwise: it shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by 0.5 before squaring, a remedy designed for small tables. Neither 8PTRZ nor 25N5D asked for the correction. The defaults of the two functions applied it, and the recorded values are the corrected ones. The cells below run both tests without it. The first three redo the comparison of 8PTRZ, and only the third, the test, prints anything.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# 8PTRZ: the replies with a greeting code, Hispanic against all other names
coded_replies <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded_replies)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)
```

The last two count the delivered emails of 25N5D and test the two proportions.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# 25N5D: the delivered emails, Hispanic against white names
counts_25n5d <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(Response_Dichotomous) & !grepl("^black", TreatmentGroup)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup),
                          greeted = Response_Dichotomous == 1 & ProperName %in% 1) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(greetings = sum(greeted), emails = n(), by = "hispanic_name")
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
prop.test(counts_25n5d$greetings, counts_25n5d$emails, correct = FALSE)
```

Without the correction the two statistics are 14.95 and 14.33. Neither changes the conclusion, but only the corrected values match the record, and the description "a chi-square test" fits both. The coding of the data matters in the same way. The z of EWFMI is positive and the z of UYV3F negative, although both describe Hispanic names greeted by name less often, because EWFMI took the Hispanic names as the base group, so that the coefficient compares white names with Hispanic names. A reproduction needs the code, or at least every default and every coding on which the code relied.

The scripts that the analysts submitted are on the OSF, in the component of the robustness study for the paper ([osf.io/38rsh](https://osf.io/38rsh/)), one sub-component for each analyst: 8PTRZ [osf.io/j8wvh](https://osf.io/j8wvh/), UYV3F [osf.io/3672s](https://osf.io/3672s/) (a review document only), EWFMI [osf.io/jhvca](https://osf.io/jhvca/), 25N5D [osf.io/v8zah](https://osf.io/v8zah/) and P9W8Y [osf.io/pzwbm](https://osf.io/pzwbm/).

## Task 4 – The menu {#task-4-menu}

This task is **exploratory**. Try several specifications and find out which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it.

`try_spec()` takes one argument for each decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), and every argument defaults to the reference specification, the raw gap of the paper: Hispanic against white names, among the replies, the five uncoded replies left out, a difference in proportions without covariates. Changing one decision means changing one argument.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Nothing changed – the reference specification.
try_spec()
```

The printout gives the shares greeted by name in the two groups, the difference in percentage points with its 95% interval, the test of the model (a *t* with HC2 standard errors for the linear model, the *z* of the logit coefficient for the logit), the number of emails analysed, the partial *r* by the conversion rule of the robustness study, the class of the result, and its place among the 64 specifications on the curve of the claim.

Each of the five cells below changes a single decision. The first two change the question that is being asked of the data, the third changes how the outcome is measured, and the last two change only how the same question is estimated. Run the five in order and compare the results.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(comparison = "nonhispanic")  # Hispanic names against white and Black names together
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(population = "all")  # every delivered email, no reply counted as no greeting
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(uncoded = "not_named")  # the five uncoded replies counted as no greeting
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(model = "logit")  # the model of the paper, as an average marginal effect
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(adjust = "place_ethnic")  # the covariates of the original model, in thirds
```

The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. `try_spec()` refuses an option that is off the curve and gives the reason. Run the cell, then edit it to try others, such as `outcome = "reply"`, `names = "male"`, `comparison = "black"`, `adjust = "acs_continuous"` or `inference = "one_tailed"`. The [decision map](menu.qmd#map) sets out every decision and its options.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(model = "three_group")
```

Then try your own combinations. The full set of arguments, each with the reference specification as its default and the options of the menu in the comment beside it:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(
  # the five decisions on which the curve keeps more than one option
  comparison = "white",      # white | nonhispanic          off the curve: black
  population = "replies",    # replies | all
  uncoded    = "drop",       # drop | not_named
  model      = "lpm",        # lpm | logit                  off the curve: three_group
  adjust     = "none",       # none | email | place | place_ethnic
                             #                              off the curve: name_sex | acs_continuous
  # the six decisions that are fixed on the curve
  outcome    = "named",      # named                        off the curve: reply | reply24
  names      = "both",       # both                         off the curve: male | female
  officials  = "any",        # any                          off the curve: hispanic
  bounced    = "exclude",    # exclude                      off the curve: no_reply
  inference  = "model",      # model                        off the curve: randomisation | chisq | one_tailed
  scale      = "pp"          # pp                           off the curve: odds_ratio | r
)
```

`my_experiments()` prints everything that you have tried, side by side, with only the decisions that you varied:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_experiments()
```

When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend, run it once more so that it is the most recent, and submit it. It appears on the live [class chart]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) as an open circle, labelled **exploratory**, with the tag that the cell prints, such as `amber-otter-42`. The tag is how you find your own marks on the chart, and your declared result in Task 5 carries the same one. To choose your own, write `submit_exploration(nickname = "...")` with a nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
submit_exploration()
```

## Task 5 – Preregistration {#task-5-preregistration}

Preregistration means setting out your choice in a plan **before** you know what it does, which stops you from quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. On this page the plan is the cell below, and `run_spec()` and `report_result()` read your choices from it. Its numbered fields follow the preregistration template of AsPredicted in a shortened form, and field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the template for secondary data (van den Akker et al. 2021).

Make one choice on each decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), complete the dotted lines, then run the cell.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: housing_emails.csv (1,014 emails, public,
#    CC0); I know that the reference specification gives -19.97 points, and
#    what my exploration in Task 4 showed.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each decision. An option that is
#    not on the curve of 64 stops prereg() with the reason why.

# The question (each of these changes what is being estimated)
my_outcome    <- "named"     # named   (greeted by name, the outcome of the claim)
my_comparison <- "white"     # white | nonhispanic   (white names, or white and Black names)
my_population <- "replies"   # replies | all   (replies only, or every delivered email)
my_names      <- "both"      # both   (male and female names pooled)
my_officials  <- "any"       # any    (replies from every official)

# Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently)
my_uncoded    <- "drop"      # drop | not_named   (the five replies without a greeting code)
my_bounced    <- "exclude"   # exclude   (the 23 emails that never arrived)

# The model (the same question and measures, another fit)
my_model      <- "lpm"       # lpm | logit   (difference in proportions, or logistic regression)
my_adjust     <- "none"      # none | email | place | place_ethnic
my_inference  <- "model"     # model   (HC2 t test, or the z test of the logit)
my_scale      <- "pp"        # pp   (percentage points)

# 4. Why this specification answers the claim, in one sentence grounded in
#    the causal graph of Task 2: .............................................
# 5. Supported if the estimate is below zero with p < .05 under the test of
#    the model; undermined if it is not significant or above zero. I will
#    report what I get.
```

Then run the cell below, which checks your choices and keeps them.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_spec <- prereg()   # checks every choice, prints your preregistration and keeps it
```

The preregistration cell, copied into your notes, is your preregistration record.

## Task 5, continued – Fit, report and place {#task-5-fit-report}

`run_spec()` fits your declared specification and prints the same lines as `try_spec()`. It refuses to run if the preregistration cell has changed since `prereg()` read it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
run_spec(my_spec)
```

The difference is in percentage points, and a value below zero means that replies to Hispanic names greeted the sender by name less often, the direction of the claim. Whether it is significant is decided by the test of the model, and the line headed `Verdict:` says which of the four cases your result falls in.

Now send it to the class chart. The cell prints your submission line and the address of a pre-filled form. Open the address in a new tab and press **Send**. Your mark joins the live [class chart]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) within seconds as a filled circle labelled **declared**, with the same tag as your exploratory result. If you have reloaded this page since Task 4, pass the tag back with `report_result(nickname = "your-tag")`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
report_result()
```

If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator, who adds your mark to the chart.

Finally, place your result on the curve of the claim: the 64 specifications that the menu keeps, ranked from the most negative estimate, with yours ringed. The first cell reads and ranks the curve, and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
spec_curve <- utils::read.csv("data/spec_curve.csv") |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("b_pp") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n(),
                          emails = factor(population, levels = c("replies", "all"),
                                          labels = c("replies only", "all delivered emails")))
```

The second picks out your specification and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
mine <- spec_curve |>
  datawizard::data_filter(comparison == my_comparison, population == my_population,
                          uncoded == my_uncoded, model == my_model, adjust == my_adjust)
```

The third draws the curve and rings yours.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank | emails, data = spec_curve, pch = 16,
                   palette = c("#0e3b6a", "#2b8585"), legend = list("right!", title = "Emails counted"),
                   ylim = c(min(spec_curve$b_pp), 0),
                   xlab = "The 64 specifications, from the most negative estimate",
                   ylab = "Hispanic minus comparison names (points)")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank, data = spec_curve, type = tinyplot::type_hline(h = 0), col = "grey60", add = TRUE)
# your specification, ringed
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank, data = mine, type = tinyplot::type_points(clim = c(3, 3)),
                   pch = 1, cex = 3, lwd = 2.5, col = "#8b1538", add = TRUE)
tinyplot::tinytheme()
```

All 64 estimates lie below zero, from −20.0 to −12.1 points, and every one of them is significant at 5% under the test of its model. The two clusters are the two answers to the decision on which emails are counted: counting every delivered email moves the estimate about 5 points towards zero, and no other decision moves it by more than about 2.7 points. Within these data the claim holds under every choice on the menu, and only its size moves. The [Class results]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) page sets the class submissions beside this curve.

A second declaration is possible: edit the preregistration cell, run it and the `prereg()` cell again, then rerun `run_spec(my_spec)`. The chart still labels it declared, but it was chosen after a result was known, as the specifications of Task 4 were, so say so wherever you write about the result.

## Task 6 – Replication {#task-6-replication}

The SCORE replication put the question of the claim to a new experiment. In 2020 it emailed 3,050 public housing authorities under four new male names, two meant to indicate Hispanic and two white senders, and the page holds the 2,717 emails that arrived, in the columns of the Housing data ([codebook](data/housing_replication_codebook.md)). `replicate_spec()` fits the specification that you declared in Task 5 on these data. The new experiment had no Black names, no reply without a greeting code and no indicator of a hard-to-find address, so the function first translates your specification and prints each change, then prints your result on the original data above your result on the new data.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
replicate_spec(my_spec)
```

Then place your result on both curves. The first cell stacks the curve of the original data, read in Task 5, and the curve of the new data, and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
replication_curve <- utils::read.csv("data/replication_curve.csv")
experiments <- c("Original experiment (2014)", "New experiment (2020)")
both <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  datawizard::data_modify(spec_curve, experiment = experiments[1]),
  replication_curve |>
    datawizard::data_filter(!duplicated(rep_spec)) |>
    datawizard::data_modify(rank = rep_rank, experiment = experiments[2],
                            emails = factor(population, levels = c("replies", "all"),
                                            labels = c("replies only", "all delivered emails")))
) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(experiment = factor(experiment, levels = experiments))
```

The second picks out your specification on each curve, translated on the new data, and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
mine_both <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  datawizard::data_modify(mine, experiment = experiments[1]),
  replication_curve |>
    datawizard::data_filter(comparison == my_comparison, population == my_population,
                            uncoded == my_uncoded, model == my_model, adjust == my_adjust) |>
    datawizard::data_modify(rank = rep_rank, experiment = experiments[2])
) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(experiment = factor(experiment, levels = experiments))
```

The third draws the two curves and rings yours on each.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8
tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank | emails, facet = ~ experiment, data = both, pch = 16,
                   facet.args = list(free = TRUE), ylim = c(min(both$b_pp) - 1, 3),
                   palette = c("#0e3b6a", "#2b8585"), legend = list("bottom!", title = "Emails counted"),
                   xlab = "Specifications, from the most negative estimate",
                   ylab = "Hispanic minus comparison names (points)")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank, facet = ~ experiment, data = both, type = tinyplot::type_hline(h = 0),
                   col = "grey60", facet.args = list(free = TRUE), add = TRUE)
# your specification, ringed on each curve; on the new data, its translation
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank, facet = ~ experiment, data = mine_both,
                   type = tinyplot::type_points(clim = c(3, 3)), pch = 1, cex = 3, lwd = 2.5,
                   col = "#8b1538", facet.args = list(free = TRUE), add = TRUE)
tinyplot::tinytheme()
```

On the new data the 12 estimates lie between −1.6 and +0.5 points, and none is significant at 5%. The vertical scale is the same in both panels. The [Class results]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) page draws the declared specifications of the class on the new data in the same way.

Write two sentences: what your result on the new data says about the claim, and how it compares with your result on the original data.

## Taking it home

This page keeps nothing once it is refreshed. The same exercise is in the [downloadable workspace]({{< var cases.housing.template-repo >}}), a folder that you open in your IDE and keep, and the [Git and GitHub module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html) shows how to put it under version control and publish its report.
